3: If peradventure the right bank so slope That we to the next Bolgia can descend, We shall escape from the imagined chase.”
7: Not yet he finished rendering such opinion, When I beheld them come with outstretched wings, Not far remote, with will to seize upon us.
11: My Leader on a sudden seized me up, Even as a mother who by noise is wakened, And close beside her sees the enkindled flames,
15: Who takes her son, and flies, and does not stop, Having more care of him than of herself, So that she clothes her only with a shift;
20: And downward from the top of the hard bank Supine he gave him to the pendent rock, That one side of the other Bolgia walls.
24: Ne’er ran so swiftly water through a sluice To turn the wheel of any land-built mill, When nearest to the paddles it approaches,
28: As did my Master down along that border, Bearing me with him on his breast away, As his own son, and not as a companion.
33: Hardly the bed of the ravine below His feet had reached, ere they had reached the hill Right over us; but he was not afraid;
37: For the high Providence, which had ordained To place them ministers of the fifth moat, The power of thence departing took from all.
41: A painted people there below we found, Who went about with footsteps very slow, Weeping and in their semblance tired and vanquished.
46: They had on mantles with the hoods low down Before their eyes, and fashioned of the cut That in Cologne they for the monks are made.
51: Without, they gilded are so that it dazzles; But inwardly all leaden and so heavy That Frederick used to put them on of straw.
55: O everlastingly fatiguing mantle! Again we turned us, still to the left hand Along with them, intent on their sad plaint;
60: But owing to the weight, that weary folk Came on so tardily, that we were new In company at each motion of the haunch.
64: Whence I unto my Leader: “See thou find Some one who may by deed or name be known, And thus in going move thine eye about.”
68: And one, who understood the Tuscan speech, Cried to us from behind: “Stay ye your feet, Ye, who so run athwart the dusky air!
72: Perhaps thou’lt have from me what thou demandest.” Whereat the Leader turned him, and said: “Wait, And then according to his pace proceed.”
77: I stopped, and two beheld I show great haste Of spirit, in their faces, to be with me; But the burden and the narrow way delayed them.
81: When they came up, long with an eye askance They scanned me without uttering a word. Then to each other turned, and said together:
86: “He by the action of his throat seems living; And if they dead are, by what privilege Go they uncovered by the heavy stole?”
90: Then said to me: “Tuscan, who to the college Of miserable hypocrites art come, Do not disdain to tell us who thou art.”
94: And I to them: “Born was I, and grew up In the great town on the fair river of Arno, And with the body am I’ve always had.
98: But who are ye, in whom there trickles down Along your cheeks such grief as I behold? And what pain is upon you, that so sparkles?”
102: And one replied to me: “These orange cloaks Are made of lead so heavy, that the weights Cause in this way their balances to creak.
106: Frati Gaudenti were we, and Bolognese; I Catalano, and he Loderingo Named, and together taken by thy city,
109:
As the wont is to take one man alone, For maintenance of its peace; and we were such That still it is apparent round Gardingo.”

“O Friars,” began I, “your iniquitous. . .” But said no more; for to mine eyes there rushed One crucified with three stakes on the ground.
113: When me he saw, he writhed himself all over, Blowing into his beard with suspirations; And the Friar Catalan, who noticed this,
117:
Said to me: “This transfixed one, whom thou seest, Counselled the Pharisees that it was meet To put one man to torture for the people.

Crosswise and naked is he on the path, As thou perceivest; and he needs must feel, Whoever passes, first how much he weighs;
122: And in like mode his father-in-law is punished Within this moat, and the others of the council, Which for the Jews was a malignant seed.”
127: And thereupon I saw Virgilius marvel O’er him who was extended on the cross So vilely in eternal banishment.
131: Then he directed to the Friar this voice: “Be not displeased, if granted thee, to tell us If to the right hand any pass slope down
136: By which we two may issue forth from here, Without constraining some of the black angels To come and extricate us from this deep.”
141: Then he made answer: “Nearer than thou hopest There is a rock, that forth from the great circle Proceeds, and crosses all the cruel valleys,
146: Save that at this ’tis broken, and does not bridge it; You will be able to mount up the ruin, That sidelong slopes and at the bottom rises.”
152:
The Leader stood awhile with head bowed down; Then said: “The business badly he recounted Who grapples with his hook the sinners yonder.”

And the Friar: “Many of the Devil’s vices Once heard I at Bologna, and among them, That he’s a liar and the father of lies.”
154: Thereat my Leader with great strides went on, Somewhat disturbed with anger in his looks; Whence from the heavy-laden I departed
156:
After the prints of his beloved feet.

Inferno: Canto XXIV
158:
In that part of the youthful year wherein The Sun his locks beneath Aquarius tempers, And now the nights draw near to half the day,

What time the hoar-frost copies on the ground The outward semblance of her sister white, But little lasts the temper of her pen,
159: The husbandman, whose forage faileth him, Rises, and looks, and seeth the champaign All gleaming white, whereat he beats his flank,
161:
Returns in doors, and up and down laments, Like a poor wretch, who knows not what to do; Then he returns and hope revives again,

Seeing the world has changed its countenance In little time, and takes his shepherd’s crook, And forth the little lambs to pasture drives.
162:
Thus did the Master fill me with alarm, When I beheld his forehead so disturbed, And to the ailment came as soon the plaster.

For as we came unto the ruined bridge, The Leader turned to me with that sweet look Which at the mountain’s foot I first beheld.
164: His arms he opened, after some advisement Within himself elected, looking first Well at the ruin, and laid hold of me.
167:
And even as he who acts and meditates, For aye it seems that he provides beforehand, So upward lifting me towards the summit

Of a huge rock, he scanned another crag, Saying: “To that one grapple afterwards, But try first if ’tis such that it will hold thee.”
169: This was no way for one clothed with a cloak; For hardly we, he light, and I pushed upward, Were able to ascend from jag to jag.
171: And had it not been, that upon that precinct Shorter was the ascent than on the other, He I know not, but I had been dead beat.
172: But because Malebolge tow’rds the mouth Of the profoundest well is all inclining, The structure of each valley doth import
173: That one bank rises and the other sinks. Still we arrived at length upon the point Wherefrom the last stone breaks itself asunder.
